newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels firmly tell U.N. envoy no ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels firmly tell U.N. envoy no ceasefire.

text.p: Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila and a roaring crowd of 10,000 supporters firmly told a U.N. envoy on Saturday there would be no ceasefire with the government before negotiations.
Kabila used his first speech since arriving in the northeastern capital of Kisangani on Friday to deliver the firm "no ceasefire" message to U.N. envoy Mohamed Sahnoun, who arrived during the rally.
"People accuse me of being an extremist because I don't want a ceasefire, but it is the people who don't want to have a ceasefire," he told Sahnoun before an estimated 10,000 people.
Sahnoun, who had just arrived by plane from Nairobi, was taken straight to the stadium where the rally was in progress and was ushered on stage during Kabila's speech but looked unperturbed.
"Do you want a ceasefire?" Kabila asked the jubilant crowd.
"Advance, forward," his boisterous supporters roared back.
"There will be no ceasefire before negotiations," Kabila earlier told reporters, sticking to his demand for talks with ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko or his representative before any truce.

Diplomats said Sahnoun, joint special envoy of the United Nations and Organisation of African Unity, was believed to be carrying new ceasefire proposals to Kabila. They said Sahnoun would probably fly to Kinshasa after talks with Kabila.
A political source told Reuters that Kabila was coming under heavy pressure to call a ceasefire, particularly after Mobutu said on Thursday he no longer ruled out talks with the rebels.

But many ordinary Zaireans, eager for a change from poverty and hardship under Mobutu, are openly rallying to Kabila, who has said the central diamond capital of Mbuji-Mayi and Zaire's second city Lubumbashi in the southeast are next in his sights.
Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) has seized more than one-fifth of Zaire, Africa's third largest country, since October.
Since the fall of Kisangani last weekend, rebels have seized Yangambi, 100 km (60 miles) west of the city and Kabinda, 100 km (60 miles) east of Mbuji-Mayi, Kabila told Saturday's rally.

In an apparent attempt to strengthen his political position before negotiations, Kabila appealed to opposition leaders to join his revolt and argued the ADFL had achieved more by taking up arms than the opposition politicians in the capital Kinshasa.
He said he demanded a transitional government composed entirely of ADFL members and any opposition politicians who did not join the rebellion would be considered Mobutu's allies.
"We are in favour of all parties who fight Mobutu, but there are ways to oppose Mobutu -- they decided to talk but we took up arms," Kabila told the crowd.
Multi-partyism was legalised in 1990 in Zaire, but since then there had been no progress in ousting Mobutu, he said.
At the rally he also delivered a strong message against France, which has backed Mobutu, who has ruled for 32 years.
He accused France in alliance with Mobutu of paying for French and other mercenaries flown in to Kisangani to bolster the Zairean army for a failed government counter-offensive in January.

Mobutu, 66, flew back to Kinshasa from France on Friday, two days after he left hospital in Monaco after fresh cancer treatment. He has spent most of his time in Europe since prostate cancer surgery in August.
Kabila said the fall of Kisangani, the greatest prize so far captured by rebels, has broken Mobutu's spell over Zaire.
During the rally, the crowd sang an insulting chorus about Mobutu's parentage and said he was no more than an assassin.

Kabila moved to bolster his already strong local support, saying he was reducing taxes on water and electricity by 50 percent. He also supervised the popular election of a new government, vice governor and city mayor before the crowd.
